summary.text: A two-year-old, healthy, male Australian Shepherd-Poodle mixed-breed dog weighing fifty-five pounds had a single verrucous or cauliflower-like papilloma, approximately 7 mm in diameter, on the external mucosal surface of the lower left lip. The owner, who brushed the dog's teeth twice daily, noticed it soon after it appeared; the dog was not on immunosuppressive medications.
The lesion was not examined histologically and had no polymerase chain reaction confirmation of canine papillomavirus. The treatment was suggested by a dentist and not reviewed with a veterinarian.

The owner held a small piece of paper towel saturated with undiluted 300 ppm molecular iodine on the lesion twice daily for 90 seconds. The lesion shrank to half its size after one week, regressed to less than half after two weeks and was nearly gone by the end of three weeks, with a small remnant shown at three weeks.

At four weeks there was no sign of the lesion, the mucosa appeared clinically healthy and there was no sign of recurrence. No adverse effect on adjacent mucosa, systemic effects or postoperative wound was noted, and no recurrence was detected clinically after one and a half years.

figures.caption_summary: Proposed mechanism of action of molecular iodine in oral papilloma resolution.Topical molecular iodine penetrates the lesion surface, producing direct antiviral and cytotoxic effects through oxidation of viral proteins and nucleic acids and disruption of infected epithelial cells [7,11]. This reduces viral load and facilitates immune system engagement, including recruitment of innate immune cells and stimulation of adaptive immunity. The combined effects result in clearance of infected tissue, followed by epithelial repair and complete clinical resolution of the papilloma [25,26].Original schematic created by the author. Mechanistic steps informed by previously published data [7,11,25,26].
